q: What does the acronym LoRA stand for in the context of fine-tuning?
options: Low-Rank Adaptation
Large Output Regression Algorithm
Layered Optimization for Reasoning Agents
Long-Range Attention
explain: LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation: it freezes the pre-trained weights and injects small trainable low-rank matrices.

q: What characterizes full fine-tuning of an LLM?
options: All model parameters are updated
All layers are frozen and only the classification head is trained
The model is quantized to 4 bits with no training
Only the model biases are updated
explain: In full fine-tuning all model weights are updated: highest potential performance but very high compute and memory costs.

q: What are adapters in parameter-efficient fine-tuning?
options: They remove entire Transformer layers to lighten the model at inference
They replace self-attention with convolutional layers in every block
Small modules inserted between layers, the only trainable parameters
They replicate the entire model with a complete separate copy for each task
explain: Adapters are small modules added between Transformer layers: only their parameters are trained, the rest stays frozen.

q: In prompt tuning (p-tuning), which parameters are optimized?
options: All model weights plus the entire vocabulary embedding matrix
Only training hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size), with no weights at all
All query/key/value attention heads of every Transformer layer
Only the continuous prompt embeddings, with the model frozen
explain: Prompt tuning freezes the model and optimizes only continuous vectors (soft prompt) concatenated with the input embeddings.

q: During EDA before fine-tuning, why analyze the distribution of text lengths?
options: To set max length, padding and truncation, and estimate memory and costs
The number of GPUs available in the distributed training cluster
The CUDA driver version installed on the GPU compute nodes
The hourly cost of the cloud instances used for distributed training
explain: EDA analyzes the length distribution to choose max sequence length, padding and truncation, and to estimate memory and costs.

q: What is the purpose of the train/validation/test split?
options: Three identical copies of the same dataset, used in parallel to speed up training
Train for training, validation for tuning and early stopping, test for final evaluation
The train set used only for testing, validation for training, and test for final validation
Three different complete models to train and compare against each other in parallel
explain: Train is for training, validation for tuning hyperparameters and deciding early stopping, test for a final unbiased estimate.

q: Which loss-curve pattern indicates overfitting?
options: Training loss and validation loss both high and flat at the end of training
Training and validation loss decreasing together without diverging
Training loss decreasing while validation loss rises
Training loss oscillating visibly due to too low a learning rate
explain: Overfitting: training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss rises; the model memorizes instead of generalizing.

q: What does underfitting indicate?
options: The model perfectly memorizes the training set but fails on validation data
The model forgets previous tasks after fine-tuning on the new domain
Weights grow out of control causing NaN values in the training loss
The model is too simple: training and validation loss both stay high
explain: Underfitting indicates a model that is too simple or undertrained: both losses stay high, the model does not capture the patterns.

q: During fine-tuning the loss oscillates wildly and does not converge. Which intervention is the priority?
options: Reduce the learning rate
Increase the number of epochs to 100
Increase the sampling temperature
Add more layers to the model
explain: Too high a learning rate takes excessively large gradient-descent steps: the loss oscillates or diverges instead of converging.

q: What is meant by batch size in training?
options: The total number of trainable parameters in the model
The number of examples processed before each weight update
The maximum number of tokens generated by the model at each inference step
The number of frozen layers not updated during PEFT fine-tuning
explain: Batch size is the number of examples processed before each weight update; large batches give more stable gradients but consume more memory.

q: What is meant by epoch in training?
options: A single weight update computed on one mini-batch
An entire inference session of the model deployed in production
One complete pass over the entire training dataset
One full learning-rate warm-up cycle at the start of training
explain: An epoch is one complete pass over the entire training dataset, with one forward and one backward pass for each batch it contains.

q: What is meant by teacher forcing in training generative models?
options: Forcing the model to always answer with the same fixed sentence, whatever the input
Training only the teacher model without ever training the student model
Using a very high learning rate in the first steps to force convergence
Feeding the decoder the previous correct tokens instead of its own predictions
explain: With teacher forcing, during training the decoder receives the previous correct tokens (ground truth) instead of its own predictions, to stabilize learning.

q: What are the roles of teacher and student in knowledge distillation?
options: The large model (teacher) transfers knowledge to a small model (student)
The small model (student) trains from scratch and supervises the large model (teacher)
Two identical models train each other on the same shared training dataset
The model is distilled by removing all attention layers from the Transformer
explain: In distillation, a large teacher model transfers its knowledge to a compact student, which costs less at inference.

q: Which statement about transfer learning is correct?
options: It completely eliminates the need to collect labeled data for the target task
It reuses pre-trained knowledge: less time, data and compute than training from scratch
It guarantees no biases inherited from pre-training in the final model
It makes the model interpretable by construction, exposing its reasoning
explain: Transfer learning reuses pre-trained weights as a starting point: it speeds up convergence and reduces data and compute versus training from scratch.

q: Which metrics should be monitored in an A/B test between two versions of an LLM in production?
options: Only the total parameter count of the two models compared in the test
Only the color and graphic style of the interface shown to evaluators
Response quality, latency, error rate, cost per query, and safety
Only the sampling temperature used during training of the two models
explain: In an LLM A/B test, monitor response quality, p50/p95 latency, error and refusal rate, cost per query, and safety signals.

q: In LoRA, what does the rank (r) hyperparameter control?
options: The number of GPUs used in the multi-node distributed training cluster
The maximum context window length the model can handle at inference
The number of learning-rate warm-up epochs at the start of training
The rank of the update matrices: higher r means more capacity and more parameters
explain: Rank r controls the size of the update matrices: higher r gives more expressive capacity but increases trainable parameters.

q: In LoRA, what is the role of the alpha hyperparameter?
options: The scaling factor of the update (scaling = alpha / r)
The number of Transformer layers the LoRA adapters are applied to
The dropout percentage applied to the LoRA adapters during training
The loss patience threshold for validation early stopping
explain: LoRA scaling is alpha divided by r: with the same r, a larger alpha amplifies the effect of the adapters on the frozen weights.

q: What distinguishes QLoRA from standard LoRA?
options: A LoRA variant that trains all model parameters in FP64 double precision
Frozen 4-bit quantized base model, plus trainable LoRA adapters
A LoRA applied only to query projections, excluding model keys and values
A proprietary NVIDIA optimizer designed for training on CPUs only
explain: QLoRA combines 4-bit quantization (NF4) of the base model with LoRA adapters: it enables fine-tuning huge models on single GPUs.

q: A vendor claims that switching to LoRA will make inference much faster. Which assessment is correct?
options: Correct assessment: inference speeds up because fewer parameters are trained
Correct assessment: lightweight adapters alone make generation faster
Correct assessment: merging is useless because LoRA already speeds up inference
Wrong assessment: LoRA alone does not speed up inference without merging
explain: Classic trap: PEFT reduces parameters, memory and storage, but does not speed up inference (adapters add operations, unless merged).

q: Which of the following statements about PEFT is FALSE?
options: PEFT trains fewer parameters than full fine-tuning
PEFT requires less VRAM and less checkpoint storage
PEFT allows serving many tasks with one base model plus lightweight adapters
PEFT always guarantees higher accuracy than full fine-tuning
explain: Exam trap: PEFT improves efficiency (fewer parameters, less memory), it does not guarantee higher accuracy than full fine-tuning.

q: A team believes LoRA removes the need for labeled data. Is that true?
options: No: a quality labeled dataset for the task is still needed
Yes: LoRA learns the new task with no labeled examples at all
Yes: pre-training alone is enough, so fine-tuning becomes unsupervised
Yes: adapters generate the correct labels for training on their own
explain: PEFT does not eliminate the need for quality labeled examples: a supervised dataset for the target task is still required.

q: Which combination best mitigates catastrophic forgetting in sequential fine-tuning?
options: Drastically increase the learning rate to adapt quickly to the new task
Use a low learning rate, PEFT, and rehearsal with data from the previous task
Remove dropout and all forms of regularization during training
Train only on the new task for many epochs with no examples of the previous one
explain: Small updates (low LR), few modified parameters (PEFT), and replaying old data preserve previous knowledge.

q: A model classified dogs and cats well, then is fine-tuned only on birds and now fails on dogs and cats. How is this diagnosed?
options: Underfitting on the new task: the model lacks capacity to learn it
Data leakage between train and test, with validation examples present in the training set
Catastrophic forgetting: the new training overwrote the old knowledge
Vanishing gradients due to overly short input sequences in the new task dataset
explain: A model trained only on new data overwrites weights important for the old task: typical catastrophic forgetting, not simple overfitting.

q: How does dropout prevent overfitting?
options: It automatically increases the learning rate at each training epoch
It freezes the base model weights and trains only the added new modules
It accumulates gradients over multiple steps to simulate large batches with little memory
It randomly disables neurons during training to reduce co-adaptation
explain: Dropout randomly disables neurons during training, preventing fragile co-adaptations and forcing the network into redundant representations.

q: What does weight decay do?
options: An L2 penalty that keeps weights small and reduces overfitting
A technique to increase batch size without additional GPU memory
A method to quantize the base model to 4 bits before fine-tuning
The schedule that gradually brings the learning rate to zero at the end of training
explain: Weight decay is an L2 penalty on weights: it keeps them small and limits model complexity, countering overfitting.

q: When is early stopping applied correctly?
options: Stopping training after a fixed number of epochs, e.g. always 100
Interrupting training when validation stops improving
Stopping production inference when latency exceeds the threshold
Interrupting learning-rate warm-up as soon as the loss starts decreasing
explain: Early stopping halts training when the validation metric stops improving, avoiding memorization of the training set.

q: What is gradient clipping for?
options: It completely zeroes the gradients of frozen layers during PEFT fine-tuning
It reduces the number of epochs needed to reach convergence
It limits gradient norms to avoid explosive updates and NaN values
It sorts gradients by importance before applying the weight update
explain: Gradient clipping limits gradient norms: it prevents explosive updates, NaNs and divergence with aggressive learning rates or noisy batches.

q: What is meant by mixed precision training?
options: Training half the epochs on one task and half on another, alternating
Halving the training dataset by discarding every other example
Training two identical models in parallel and averaging their final weights
Using FP16/BF16 for compute and memory, with master copies in FP32
explain: Mixed precision uses FP16/BF16 for most computations (less memory, faster on Tensor Cores) while keeping FP32 master copies for stability.

q: What is the difference between data parallelism and model parallelism?
options: Data parallelism: replicated model and split data; model parallelism: split model
Data parallelism partitions weights across GPUs, model parallelism replicates data on each
They are two different names for the same CPU-offload technique
Data parallelism is only for inference and model parallelism only for initial EDA
explain: Data parallelism: each GPU holds a replica of the model and processes different batches. Model parallelism: the model is partitioned across GPUs.

q: With micro-batch 4 and gradient accumulation every 8 steps, what is the effective batch size?
options: 8, because only the number of accumulation steps counts in the calculation
16, computed as the arithmetic mean of 4 and 8
32, the product of micro-batch and accumulation steps
256, computed as the square of 8 times 4
explain: The effective batch is micro-batch times accumulation steps: 4 times 8 equals 32, simulating a large batch with little memory.

q: What do cosine decay and linear decay describe in learning-rate scheduling?
options: Two different dedicated optimizers, one for LoRA and one for full fine-tuning
Two distinct loss functions, one for training and one for model validation
Two schedules that reduce the learning rate after warm-up (cosine vs linear)
Two types of weight quantization, at 4 and 8 bits respectively
explain: Cosine decay reduces the LR following a cosine down to near zero; linear decay reduces it linearly. Both refine convergence after warm-up.

q: Which practice is a valid example of data augmentation for NLP?
options: Duplicating the exact same examples a thousand times with no variation
Collecting test data and using it directly for model training
Normalizing model weights after each training epoch
Generating realistic text variants (paraphrases, back-translation)
explain: Paraphrasing, back-translation and synonym substitutions generate realistic variants that make the model robust without collecting new data.

q: How is class imbalance handled in the fine-tuning dataset?
options: Resample, use class weights, and evaluate with F1/AUC in addition to accuracy
Remove the minority class entirely from the fine-tuning dataset
Increase the learning rate until it compensates the class imbalance in the dataset
Use accuracy as the only model evaluation metric
explain: With imbalanced classes, resample, use class weights or focal losses, and evaluate with F1/AUC rather than accuracy alone.

q: Why is deduplication important in preprocessing?
options: To artificially increase the number of training epochs without new data
To remove duplicates: they waste compute, inflate metrics, and risk leakage
To automatically reduce the learning rate during training epochs
To convert the model to low-precision quantized format before deployment
explain: Duplicates waste compute, inflate metrics, and can cause train/test leakage: deduplication cleans the signal.

q: What is the main purpose of knowledge distillation before deployment?
options: To increase the parameter count of the final production model
To improve teacher accuracy using student predictions
To obtain a small, cheap student with quality close to the teacher
To eliminate the validation phase from the distilled student training
explain: The primary goal of distillation is a small, cheap-to-serve student that retains most of the teacher's quality.

q: After LoRA fine-tuning, the team wants to eliminate the extra adapter latency at inference without losing the adaptation. Which operation is correct?
options: Re-train the whole model from scratch in full precision with a new complete training run
Fuse (merge) the adapter weights into the base weights with merge_and_unload
Increase the rank r after training with no retraining at all
Convert the trained adapters into discrete natural-language text prompts
explain: Trained LoRA adapters can be fused into the frozen weights (merge_and_unload): the resulting model behaves as adapted but with no extra branches at inference.

q: A team with 1x 24 GB GPU must adapt a 70B LLM to a specialist domain. Which strategy is realistic?
options: 4-bit QLoRA with adapters and accumulation, few epochs with validation
Training the model from scratch on the single 24 GB GPU available
Increasing the learning rate 10x to compensate for reduced memory
Full 32-bit fine-tuning with batch size 64 and 50 epochs on the single GPU
explain: A 70B model does not fit in 24 GB in full fine-tuning: 4-bit QLoRA plus adapters, mixed precision and accumulation make the task feasible.

q: Train loss keeps falling until the end of training but validation loss rises after epoch 3. Diagnosis and remedy?
options: Increase the learning rate and continue training for 20 more epochs
Early stopping plus regularization (dropout, weight decay) or more data
Freeze the validation set and continue on train loss only, ignoring the divergence
Switch to a 10x larger model with no other changes
explain: Train/val divergence after epoch 3 is emerging overfitting: stop with early stopping and increase regularization or data.

q: During training, NaN losses and gradient explosions appear. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Double the batch size and triple the learning rate to stabilize the loss
Disable all monitoring logs and continue training until convergence
Gradient clipping, lower LR with warm-up, and checking data and precision
Increase the sampling temperature used during generation
explain: NaN loss and explosions indicate unstable gradients: clipping, a lower LR with warm-up, and checking mixed precision and corrupted data.

q: What is the difference between rehearsal (replay) and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) against forgetting?
options: Rehearsal increases the learning rate while EWC zeroes it entirely
Rehearsal removes old data while EWC duplicates it in training
Rehearsal freezes the entire model while EWC unfreezes all layers
Rehearsal replays old data; EWC constrains weights important in the past
explain: Rehearsal mixes examples of the old task into the new-task training; EWC penalizes changes to weights important for past tasks.

q: After 2 days of A/B testing on 200 queries, model B shows +2% approval. What should the team do?
options: Declare B the winner because the +2% observed on 200 queries is certainly significant
Conclude that A and B are equivalent without analyzing user segments and use cases
Check significance and power with an adequate sample and duration before promoting B
Stop the test on the first day B beats A, without waiting for the planned duration
explain: A valid A/B test requires a hypothesis, a primary metric, statistical power and sufficient duration: +2% on 200 queries is rarely significant.

q: A fine-tuning run with a high learning rate diverges within the first 100 steps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: The batch size chosen was too small for the validation set used in the test
Early divergence from high LR without warm-up: the initial ramp is needed
More dropout applied at inference is necessarily missing
The sampling temperature used in generation was too low
explain: Without warm-up, a high LR in the first steps with unstable weights and statistics causes early divergence; the initial ramp prevents it.

q: A company wants to serve 20 tasks with a single base model. Which statement about LoRA, prompt tuning and prefix tuning is correct?
options: They are three different names for classic full fine-tuning on all weights
LoRA: low-rank in weights; prompt tuning: soft prompt; prefix: per-layer vectors
Prompt tuning updates all 70 billion parameters of the base model
Each adapter always requires a different separate base model for each task served
explain: LoRA modifies weights via low-rank matrices, prompt tuning acts on inputs, prefix tuning on the keys/values of each layer; all favor multi-task serving on a single base model.

q: A 70B model in FP32 does not fit on a 24 GB GPU even with batch 1. Which architectural solution is correct?
options: Increase the number of epochs until the model fits into GPU memory
Use only data parallelism, replicating the whole model on each available cluster GPU
Add more training data to reduce the memory footprint
Partition the model across GPUs (model parallelism), with quantization and offload
explain: If the model does not fit on one GPU, model/tensor/pipeline parallelism or offload/quantization are needed; data parallelism alone replicates the model and is not enough.

q: EDA reveals the dataset over-represents one demographic group and contains offensive jokes. What is the correct response before fine-tuning?
options: Rebalance and filter the data, evaluate fairness, and monitor the deployment
Ignore the issue because transfer learning alone removes inherited biases
Simply increase training epochs on the skewed dataset
Remove the validation split to train on more data, even if skewed
explain: If EDA shows imbalances and offensive content, fine-tuning amplifies them: rebalancing, filtering, fairness evaluations and post-deployment monitoring are needed.

q: During LLM pre-training, which objective is optimized?
options: Classifying each sentence into predefined categories assigned by human annotators
Predicting the next token given the previous context
Sorting the corpus documents by their publication date
Quantizing the weights to 4 bits before starting training
explain: Pre-training uses causal language modeling: the model learns to predict the next token given the context, with no manual labels.

q: What does a typical supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset look like?
options: Instruction/response pairs showing the desired behavior
Raw unstructured text, like that used in pre-training
Only numeric class labels with no example text at all
Response pairs ranked by preference with reward scores
explain: The SFT dataset contains demonstration examples in instruction/response format: the model learns to imitate the desired behavior.

q: What are the three stages of RLHF, in the correct order?
options: Reward model, pre-training from scratch, quantization of the final model
SFT, reward-model training, optimization with RL
Optimization with RL, preference collection, concluding SFT
Instruction tuning, weight pruning, distillation onto the student
explain: RLHF proceeds in three stages: demonstrative SFT, reward-model training on preference-ranked responses, policy optimization with reinforcement learning.

q: An assistant must answer with data updated daily (prices, regulations). Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Full fine-tuning redone every single night
Training from scratch every week on the entire text corpus
RAG with sources updated at query time
Raised sampling temperature to stimulate memory
explain: For fast-changing knowledge, RAG retrieves up-to-date facts at query time: redoing fine-tuning every day would be costly and fragile.

q: What does the data for training a reward model look like?
options: Raw text taken from the web with no filtering
Sentences labeled with the grammatical class of each word
Single instruction/response pairs with no comparison
Responses compared and ranked by human preference
explain: The reward model learns from comparisons: for each prompt, two ranked responses (preferred vs rejected) according to human judgment.

q: After adaptation on new data only, the model excels on the new task but collapses on previous ones. What is this phenomenon called?
options: Loss of checkpoints due to a storage disk failure
Catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge
Loss collapsing to zero after the very first epoch
Random resetting of weights at every optimization step
explain: Training only on new data, the model overwrites weights useful for previous tasks and degrades on them: this is catastrophic forgetting.

q: Training converges but extremely slowly, with minimal improvement each epoch. Most likely cause?
options: Oversized batch size making gradients too noisy
Sampling temperature set to too high a value
Learning rate too low, with tiny update steps
Aggressive dropout wrongly applied at inference
explain: Too low a learning rate takes tiny steps: the loss decreases but very slowly, wasting epochs and compute.

q: How is the perplexity of a language model interpreted?
options: High values indicate more creative and diverse responses
It measures GPU memory used during distributed training
It counts the number of trainable parameters in the model
Low values indicate better predictive ability on text
explain: Perplexity measures the average uncertainty in predicting the next token: the lower it is, the better the model predicts text.

q: What does temperature control in text generation?
options: The maximum number of tokens that can be generated in a response
Randomness: low is more deterministic, high is more varied
The GPU memory allocated to hold the KV-cache
The number of documents retrieved from the vector database
explain: Temperature scales the logits before sampling: low values make output deterministic, high values more creative but less predictable.

q: A fine-tuning run on a small dataset continues for 50 epochs and train loss reaches near zero. What happened?
options: The model memorized the examples instead of generalizing
It achieved perfect alignment with human preferences
The learning rate self-zeroed when warm-up completed
The weights self-quantized to exactly 4 bits
explain: Too many epochs on little data lead to memorization: near-zero train loss with an expected collapse on validation metrics.

q: Few-shot prompting is not enough: dozens of examples would be needed to describe the task. What should be considered?
options: Raise the temperature until the answer appears by chance
Bake the behavior into the weights with fine-tuning
Repeat the same prompt hundreds of times until it works
Shrink the context window to force short answers
explain: When the task requires too many in-prompt examples (cost, latency, context limit), fine-tuning bakes the behavior into the weights in a stable way.

q: What are checkpoints saved during training for?
options: To resume training and restore the best epoch
To generate more creative responses at inference
To replace the validation set in final evaluation
To remove duplicate texts present in the dataset
explain: Checkpoints save weights and optimizer state: they allow resuming after interruptions, comparing epochs, and rolling back to the best version.

Policy optimization with reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-model training
Reward-model training, policy optimization with reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), policy optimization with reinforcement learning, reward-model training

To teach the model to follow natural-language instructions and generalize to unseen tasks

options: DPO directly optimizes the policy on preference pairs without training an explicit reward model or using reinforcement learning
DPO always requires a separate reward model larger than the policy being optimized
DPO uses only prompts with no responses and no human preference data
DPO freezes the entire model and updates only the input tokens

explain: In RLAIF an LLM judge produces the preference labels, reducing human-annotation cost and time while keeping the RLHF scheme.

A variant of RLHF in which preference feedback is generated by an AI model instead of human annotators
A quantization technique that uses AI to shrink weights to 4 bits
An attack in which one model steals the rewards of another model
q: What is meant by RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback)?

The model runs out of memory because the batch size is excessive
The model produces verbose, flattering responses that earn high reward without being truly more useful or correct

options: Because LoRA increases all model parameters to memorize more examples
Because LoRA always requires more memory than full fine-tuning but converges sooner
Because LoRA eliminates the need for any supervised training data
Because LoRA updates only small low-rank adapters, reducing memory, storage and overfitting risk
q: A team wants to adapt a 70B LLM to a business task with a single GPU and little data. Why is LoRA/PEFT preferable to full fine-tuning?

explain: Freezing the backbone keeps the representation learned in pre-training fixed and updates only a few new parameters, with more stable and cheaper training.
options: Leaving the pre-trained model weights unchanged and training only the added head or adapters
Zeroing all model weights before each training epoch
Running inference at zero temperature with no sampling
Removing attention layers to speed up training
q: What does freezing the backbone mean during LLM fine-tuning?

options: To sort generated tokens by vocabulary frequency
To limit overly aggressive policy updates and keep training stable near the current policy
To cut the maximum length of model-generated responses
To remove the KL penalty term and maximize only the raw reward

options: It ignores the rejected response and maximizes only the preferred one's likelihood
It minimizes the likelihood of both responses to regularize the model
It increases the log-probability margin of the preferred response over the rejected one, anchored to the reference model
It assigns the same probability target to both responses in the comparison
